clue.text: Chap after water-biscuit

indicators.note: the chap's name is placed after the water, so the two pieces come in that order

parts.note: a bath is a tub of water, so water gives BATH
Oliver is a man's name, standing for any chap

explanation.surface: A man follows something to do with water and a biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a traditional British plain cracker first made in the city of Bath. 'water' tempts you to read 'water-biscuit' as the definition, but the hyphen is the surface's trick.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a named brand of dry cracker, so it is one kind of biscuit.

clue.text: Sprinkle venerable historian with just a drop of water

parts.note: the Venerable Bede was the Anglo-Saxon monk who wrote an early history of England

indicators.note: only a drop of the word is taken, meaning its opening letter alone

explanation.surface: Someone sprinkles an old historian with a little water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just a drop of' takes only the first letter, W, of 'water'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedew is to wet lightly with drops, as dew does, so it means sprinkle.

clue.text: Show them one cocktail leads to trouble

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one
read as cock-tail, the tail or final letter of the word cock
ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Giving people a single cocktail is asking for trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cocktail' splits into 'cock' and 'tail': the tail of COCK is K. 'leads to' just joins the pieces. The answer is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a comic opera staged in theatres, so it is a stage show.

clue.text: Like Nelson, in part, and often seen in casinos

definitions.text: Like Nelson, in part, and often seen in casinos

parts.words: Like Nelson, in part, and often seen in casinos
parts.note: Admiral Nelson lost an arm, so part of the phrase describes him, and the whole phrase is a gambling machine with a lever found in casinos

explanation.surface: Something resembles the admiral and turns up in gambling halls.
explanation.walkthrough: Nelson, Britain's most famous admiral, lost his right arm in battle; the slot machine gets its nickname from its single lever and the way it takes your money.
explanation.definitionFit: A slot machine with a pull handle is nicknamed this, and gambling halls are full of them.

clue.text: Break in an untried version

indicators.note: a version is a new arrangement of something, so the letters of untried are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone breaks into a new, unproven version of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version' rearranges the letters of UNTRIED.
explanation.definitionFit: To intrude is to force your way in uninvited, which is to break in.

clue.text: These days, gold money is put first by country

indicators.note: the money is placed at the front, ahead of the other two pieces

parts.note: the ecu was a European currency unit, so money gives ECU
AD, anno Domini, labels years of the present era
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: Nowadays a nation prioritises gold and money.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the money last, but 'is put first' places it at the front of the country's name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a South American republic on the equator.

clue.text: Gentleman, one about to make a bloomer

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the pieces before it are read backwards

parts.note: Sir is the title or form of address for a gentleman
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gentleman is on the verge of making a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns SIRI round. 'bloomer' looks like a mistake, but here it is a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a flowering plant, so in crossword terms something that blooms.

clue.text: Gear I finally found to be stiff

parts.note: a rig is a set of equipment or gear

indicators.note: finally takes the closing letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Equipment turns out to be stiff once found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives D, the last letter of 'found'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigid means inflexible, unbending.

clue.text: Half a day considered very wet

indicators.note: half of the day's name is kept, the front part of the word

parts.note: Saturday is a day of the week
to rate something is to consider or judge it

explanation.surface: Something is judged to be soaking for half the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half a' keeps SATUR, the first half of SATURDAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Soaked through completely is extremely wet.

clue.text: A tar's not in port when at sea, being taken abroad

indicators.note: at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A sailor away from harbour is on his way to foreign parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when at sea' rearranges the letters of A TARS NOT IN PORT. Historically convicts were sent overseas to penal colonies as a punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Shipping convicts overseas to colonies was the punishment of being sent away abroad.

clue.text: Nearest the bottom in river — a bore

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Britain
a pest is a nuisance or bore

explanation.surface: A tidal wave on a river reaches the lowest part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' hints at a tidal wave running up a river, but it means a nuisance.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of deep describes whatever lies lowest, closest to the floor.

clue.text: Just a piano

definitions.meaning: fair and honest, a person of integrity
a piano whose strings run vertically, as opposed to a grand

explanation.definitionFit: An honest person is called upright, and an upright is a vertical piano.

clue.text: Bind about a request for contributions

parts.note: to whip a rope is to bind its end with twine
round and about both mean around

explanation.surface: Someone tied up asks people to chip in.
explanation.walkthrough: To whip a rope's end is to bind it tightly with cord. A WHIP-ROUND is a British informal collection of money, e.g. for a colleague's leaving present.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an informal collection where people chip in money, so an appeal for donations.

clue.text: Ruined — and I, at the outset, reached rock-bottom

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters of and I are rearranged
at the outset means at the start, taking the first letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Someone says they were ruined and hit rock bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruined' rearranges AND I to NADI; 'at the outset' gives R from 'reached'.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point of anything, its very depths.

clue.text: Weigh a piece of fish

definitions.meaning: to weigh, as on a balance that measures mass
one of the thin plates covering a fish's skin

explanation.definitionFit: A balance for weighing is a scale, and a fish's skin is covered in small flat plates of that name.

clue.text: Found grass to start operations

parts.note: to found an organisation is to set it up
in British slang to grass on or shop someone is to inform on them to the police

explanation.surface: Someone discovers turf before getting a business going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' is not the past of find but 'establish'; 'grass' is British slang for informing, which is also 'shop'.
explanation.definitionFit: To open a business is to begin trading, the idiom meaning to get going.

clue.text: In close touch with partner swimming around the river

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go around the river's name, which sits inside them
swimming means moving freely, so the letters of partner are jumbled

parts.note: the Po is the major river of Italy, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: Someone stays close to their partner as they swim around the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swimming' rearranges the partner's letters to ENRAPRT, and the river sits inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: A French phrase meaning in harmony or in close communication with someone.

clue.text: Pat's too Italian to be upset over an article in French

indicators.note: in a down entry the first part sits over, above, the second
in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: troppo is the Italian word for too
une is a French indefinite article

explanation.surface: Pat is too Italian to get upset about a French newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be upset' reverses TROPPO to OPPORT, placed 'over' UNE. 'Pat' looks like a name, but as an adjective it means well-timed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pat as an adjective means timely, coming at just the right moment.

clue.text: Disorderly louts rob you, we hear, in a riot

indicators.note: a riot is wild disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new order
we hear signals that a word is replaced by the letter that sounds like it

parts.note: the letter U is pronounced the same as you

explanation.surface: Thugs rob you during a disorderly riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns 'you' into U; 'in a riot' rearranges LOUTS ROB plus U.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for turbulent and unruly, full of disturbance.

clue.text: Figure of eight

parts.note: not the looping shape but a geometric figure with eight sides

explanation.definitionFit: A plane shape with eight sides and eight angles is a figure of eight sides.

clue.text: Place in the South that's tidied up its centre

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as printed 'Place in the South that's tidied up its centre (7)' for SITUATE: S is the South, but no reading of 'that's tidied up its centre' gives ITUATE, and no source gives the parse
annotationWithheld.clue: Place in the South that's tidied up its centre

clue.text: Fleet's in front of the pongoes in the attack

indicators.note: the letter goes inside the word for the attack

parts.note: a raid is an attack

indicators.note: the front of the word that follows is its opening letter, here the start of the soldiers' nickname

explanation.surface: The navy goes ahead of the army in the assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' looks like ships, but it means fast. 'front of the' gives P from 'pongoes' (old British forces slang for soldiers), and 'in' puts it inside RAID.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet as an adjective means swift.

clue.text: Heathen god accepts silver

indicators.note: accepts means takes in, so one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A deity takes silver from an unbeliever.
explanation.walkthrough: The god is the Greek nature god, and silver is given by its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone outside the main world religions is an unbeliever or heathen.

clue.text: Make a noise — a big noise

indicators.note: noise here signals that a word is taken by its spoken sound

parts.note: great means big

explanation.surface: Someone tells you to make a noise, and a loud one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noise' hints that 'big' (GREAT) is heard, which is how the answer is pronounced.
explanation.definitionFit: To grate is to make a harsh rasping sound.

clue.text: Word (4)

parts.note: the bracketed count describes a word made up of four letters, rather than giving the length of this entry

explanation.definitionFit: From Greek tetra-, four, and gramma, letter: a term of four letters.

clue.text: Note inserted in test piece of music

indicators.note: inserted in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the MOT is the annual British roadworthiness test for vehicles
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A musical note is slipped into an exam piece.
explanation.walkthrough: The test is the MOT, the yearly UK roadworthiness check for cars; the note goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A short choral composition for church use is one kind of musical work.

clue.text: Trial making sense

definitions.meaning: a court case or session before a judge
one of the five senses, perceiving sound

explanation.definitionFit: A court case is a hearing, and the ability to perceive sound is the sense of hearing.

clue.text: That will go in the alkali quota

definitions.text: That will go in the alkali quota

indicators.note: the answer goes inside the words that follow, sitting within their letters

explanation.surface: Something will be added to the alkali quota.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in alkALI QUOTa. In maths, an aliquot is a part that divides a whole exactly, so it will 'go into' it.
explanation.definitionFit: An aliquot is a portion that divides into a quantity exactly, a measured sample of it.

clue.text: PM in IOM

definitions.meaning: Sir Robert ... was a nineteenth-century British Prime Minister
IOM is the Isle of Man, and this is a town on its west coast

explanation.definitionFit: Robert Peel served as Prime Minister, and a harbour town on the Isle of Man bears the same name.

clue.text: In detention, one after another intended to be heard

indicators.note: to be heard signals that the pieces are said aloud and the answer is what is heard

parts.note: in turn means one after another; meant means intended

explanation.surface: In custody, prisoners take turns to be heard.
explanation.walkthrough: IN TURN MEANT, spoken, sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding people in confinement without trial, especially in wartime, is a form of detention.
